full_text:
**Verdict: KNOWN.** Masuko et al. (2017) studied this model class and reported the same behaviour.

**1. Model family.** This is the "group chase and escape" model, a lattice agent-based model from statistical physics and nonlinear science. Each chaser moves toward its nearest target, and each target moves away from its nearest chaser. Kamimura & Ohira introduced it.

**2. The specific behaviour.** The lazy-chaser variant is the match. Masuko, Hiraoka, Ito and Shimada put random-walking chasers into this model on a periodic square lattice. They measured the total time T to catch all targets, averaged over runs. Their findings line up with your observations:
- **Uniform laziness gives no gain.** Laziness is introduced as random walks in two ways, uniformly and in a "division of labor" way. The uniform way is always ineffective. This matches your `gain_if_all_sometimes_random = 0`.
- **Division of labor can help.** The division-of-labor way can improve catching efficiency, through a pincer attack by diligent and lazy chasers. In that scheme, a fixed fraction R of chasers always random-walk and the rest always chase the nearest target. This is your 30% random movers.
- **The tail gets shorter.** Replacing some chasers with random walkers suppresses the tail of the distribution and makes unlucky cases rarer, with a slight increase in the peak position. This matches your typical time of about 1000 versus rare runs of about 10000, and the lower mean at 30%.
- **The mechanism is the same.** Chasers that follow the same target from the same direction form a cluster, and a cluster rarely scatters. A random-walking chaser can draw the evader toward the cluster, because the evader flees from the random walker as its nearest chaser.
- **Standing still was also tested.** The paper replaced the lazy chasers with fixed ones that don't move at all. This corresponds to your "standing still" variant. I did not read the result.

The base model with the nearest-target rule on a lattice comes from Kamimura & Ohira. They found cases where an optimal number of chasers exists, and signs of self-organised spatial structures. The same paper reports heavy-tailed catch-time distributions (the search snippet mentions log-normal-like shapes).

**3. Verified citations** (title, authors, year and venue checked against search results):
- Kamimura A., Ohira T. (2010), "Group chase and escape", *New J. Phys.* 12, 053013. Published 10 May 2010. The arXiv version is 0912.4327.
- Masuko M., Hiraoka T., Ito N., Shimada T. (2017), "The effect of laziness in group chase and escape", *J. Phys. Soc. Jpn.* 86, 085002. The arXiv preprint is 1612.04556, titled "The effect of laziness in chasers in group chase and escape model". The journal reference is confirmed on the arXiv abstract page.
- Review: Kamimura & Ohira, *Group Chase and Escape: Fusion of Pursuits-Escapes and Collective Motions* (Springer, 2019), a book. Google Scholar lists it and the Ohira homepage confirms it. I did not read it. A shorter review is Hiraoka-adjacent work by Ohira's group: Springer's *Artificial Life and Robotics* article "Collective behaviors emerging from chases and escapes" (2023) cites the laziness paper, but I only saw its reference list.

**4. Differences from your system.** These probably don't matter, but I could not confirm all of them.
- **Details I could not check.** Masuko et al. use their own lattice size and density, and the snippets don't show their update order or exclusion rule. Your 200×200 lattice at density 0.001 and your sequential random-order update with exclusion may differ.
- **Distance metric.** I did not confirm whether theirs is Euclidean, as yours is.
- **Optimal share.** I did not see their optimal R. Your 0.3 optimum and mean times of 3100 and 1380 are system-specific numbers that I could not compare.
- **Uniform laziness.** Their uniform case is a per-step random-walk probability P for every chaser, which is the "all sometimes random" case.

**5. Confidence: medium-high.** The model, the observable, the uniform-versus-division-of-labor contrast, the tail suppression and the clustering mechanism all match. I held back from "high" because I read only the arXiv text and snippets, not the full paper. I also couldn't check the exact optimum R or the lattice parameters.
